units.translation: With the prepositions ἀνά [up], ἀντί [against], ἀπό [from], ἐκ [out of], ἐπί [upon] and words compounded with these prepositions, into κἀνά, κἀντί, κἀκ (or κἀξ), κἀπό, κἀπί (both with elision κἀπ᾿ and before an aspirated letter καφ᾿), for example
With other words beginning with short a, as κἀγαθούς [and good (acc. pl.)], κἀγκυλητά [and crooked (neut. pl.)], κἀγρίοις [and wild (dat. pl.)], κἀκροθίνια [and first-fruits]

With words beginning with e, as κἀγώ [and I], κἄγωγε [and I at least], κἀμοῦ [and of me], κἀμοί [and to me], κἄμοιγε [and to me at least], κἀμέ [and me], κἀμός [and my], κἀκεῖνος [and that one], κἀντεῦθεν [and from there], κάπειτα [and then], κάτι [and something], and others, very often also with the augment, as κἀγένοντο [and they became], κάζευζα [and I yoked], κάπράϋνε [and he softened], κἀφρένωσας [and you made wise]. Crasis with ἑκατόν [hundred] may seem to be restored in the words (fr. 181) which the epitomator of Athenaeus 1 p. 11ο brought in a metrically resolved form: καὶ ἑκατοντάρχας [and centurions], where Porson, as I said above, wrote κἀκατοντάρχας.
With η it is not contracted except with the article χὴ (Doric χἀ) for καὶ ἡ [and the (fem.)] and the pronoun ἡμεῖς [we] and its oblique cases.

With ο it is contracted in the article χὠ for καὶ ὁ [and the (masc.)], on which see Trypho in Apollonius on adverbs p. 496, 30. Likewise χὤστις [and whoever], χὤτι [and that], χὔτε [and when], and χώπη [and where].
With υ in the pronoun χύμεῖς for καὶ ὑμεῖς [and you (pl.)]
With ω
With the dative ᾧ [to whom]

With a diphthong it does not coalesce except with the article χαί for καὶ αἱ [and the (fem. pl.)], except that καὶ αἰσχρῶν [and of shameful things] is read contracted as κάσχρῶν in Sept. 685, while in the apographs of Met it is written καἰσχρῶν.

Finally it must be noted that in anapaests where καί [and] is read before a short vowel it is sometimes uncertain among the scenic poets whether crasis is to be employed or the diphthong shortened, as καὶ ἀκοντισταί [and javelin-throwers] Pers. 52 and καὶ ἀμηνίτῳ [and to the unangered] Suppl. 975, from which it does not follow that Pers. 546 κἀγὼ δὲ μόρον [and I my fate] should be changed to καὶ ἐγώ, since κἀγώ, which is very frequent in dialogue, may also have been preferred in anapaests over καὶ ἐγώ.
a conjunctive particle, like Latin et, serving to connect two words or sentences or parts of sentences.

Thus M, from which an ancient hand made καὶ τὰν ῥίψοπλον [and the shield-casting (acc.)], which passed into the apographs. But what I restored is undoubtedly correct: ἀνδρολέτειραν νόσον, ῥίψοπλον ἄταν [man-destroying plague, shield-casting ruin].

where Hermann indicated a lacuna. For words pertaining to the meaning of the name Ἐτεοκλέους [of Eteocles] have fallen out, just as πολυνεικεῖς [strife-loving] pertains to the name Πολυνείκους [of Polyneices].
thus I wrote for τοῖσδε [these (dat.)]
thus Porson for καί [and]
the former verse is quoted by Stobaeus 39, 14 as attributed to Sophocles: the latter verse I said in my note on Clement of Alexandria, vol. 3 p. 127, does not seem to be Aeschylus's.
ὥστε κἀπαρκεῖν εὖ πραπίδων λαχόντα [so that even to suffice well for one who has obtained wisdom], from Triclinius's conjecture for ὥστ᾽ ἀπαρκεῖν [so as to suffice].
Frequent in all writers is καὶ ταῦτα [and these things], corresponding to Latin idque.
where to Prometheus saying πρὸς τοῖσδε μέντοι πῦρ ἐγώ σφιν ώπασα [besides these things, I gave them fire], the chorus responds
and thus ἄλλως τε καί [especially and]
Furthermore
where ἢ καί [or also], as often, corresponds to the preceding καί [and].
thus Wunderlich for κἀμέ [and me]
